7. Tidying the Data with mutate()
#| eval: false
tracts <- raw_tracts %>%
  mutate(
    rent         = rentE,
    rent_moe     = rentM,
    income       = incomeE,
    building_age = 2023 - year_builtE,
    pct_renters  = renters / total_hh * 100,
    dist_ch_mi   = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, city_hall)) / 5280
  ) %>%
  select(GEOID, rent, rent_moe, income, building_age,
         pct_renters, dist_ch_mi) %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(rent),
    !is.na(income),
    !is.na(building_age),
    !is.na(pct_renters)
  )



New variable
Calculation




building_age
2023 (ACS year) − median year built


pct_renters
renter households ÷ total households × 100


dist_ch_mi
distance to City Hall in feet ÷ 5,280



There are 5,280 feet in a mile.
as.numeric() drops the units attached by st_distance() and returns a plain number.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
8. Why Drop Missing Values First?
In R:
!
means NOT. So !is.na(rent) keeps records where rent is not missing.
If a row has a missing value, lm() will quietly drop it, without telling you.
That creates a problem:

Different models could be estimated on different sets of tracts, so their RMSEs would not be directly comparable.

For fair comparisons, every model must use:

Exactly the same records
Exactly the same folds

After filtering, the dataset has:

377 census tracts

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
9. A Consistent Cross-Validation Helper Function

Goal
This week we want to see how changing the features changes the same model.
So we remove randomness in the fold assignment:

If a tract is in fold 1 the first time, it stays in fold 1 every time.

The caret package can also do train/test splits. Here, however, fixing the folds ourselves guarantees identical comparisons.


Setting the folds
#| eval: false
set.seed(5080)

folds <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(tracts)))
set.seed() makes the random number generator reproducible. The course number, 5080, is used as the seed.
This randomly assigns each tract to one of 10 folds.


The function
#| eval: false
cv_rmse <- function(f, data, log_y = FALSE) {

  preds <- rep(NA, nrow(data))

  for (k in 1:10) {
    # Train on every fold except k
    m <- lm(f, data = data[folds != k, ])

    # Predict for the held-out fold k
    preds[folds == k] <- predict(m, newdata = data[folds == k, ])
  }

  # If the outcome was logged, convert predictions back to dollars
  if (log_y) preds <- exp(preds)

  sqrt(mean((data$rent - preds)^2))
}


How it works
For each fold k:
Fold k steps aside (test set)
        ↓
Fit lm() on all other folds (training set) → model m
        ↓
predict() rents for fold k using m's coefficients
        ↓
Compare predictions with actual rents
Every tract gets a turn in the test set.
A function is just a set of instructions that runs whenever it is called. Here we give it:

f: the regression formula
data: the dataset
log_y: whether the outcome was logged (explained in Section 14)

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
10. Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)
\[
RMSE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2}
\]
where:

\(y_i\) = actual rent
\(\hat{y}_i\) = predicted rent

RMSE is in the same units as the outcome: dollars of rent.

Lower RMSE = better out-of-sample prediction.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
section: 11. The Baseline Model and the Model Log
text:
11. The Baseline Model and the Model Log
A model log is simply a record of each model and its result.

“Log” here means a record, not a logarithm.

It is stored as a tibble, and we add a row for every new model.
#| eval: false
f0 <- rent ~ income + pct_renters + building_age + dist_ch_mi

m0 <- lm(f0, data = tracts)

model_log <- tibble(
  model = "M0: Baseline",
  rmse  = cv_rmse(f0, tracts)
)
The baseline predicts rent as a function of:

Median household income
Percent renters
Building age
Distance to City Hall


Result

Baseline RMSE ≈ $265

On average, the baseline prediction for a tract’s median rent is off by about $265.
Is that good enough? The lecture’s answer: “I don’t know, I’m not your boss.”

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
12. Trick 1: Log Transformations

When to use a log
1. Skewed distributions
If a variable has a long tail rather than a roughly normal distribution, taking the log can help. Linear regression works best with roughly normal data.
2. Theoretical reasons: percentage change matters
Consider income:









Change
Raw increase
Percentage change
Meaning




$30,000 → $60,000
+$30,000
+100%
Income doubles. A neighbourhood may move out of poverty


$170,000 → $200,000
+$30,000
≈ +18%
A modest bonus



The raw increase is identical, but the consequences are very different.

When percentage changes matter more than unit changes, consider a log.



Workflow
Look at the distribution
        ↓
Does it look skewed?
        ↓
Try a log and compare cross-validated RMSE

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
13. Logging a Predictor
The outcome (rent) stays the same. Simply write log() in the formula:
#| eval: false
f1 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age + dist_ch_mi

m1 <- lm(f1, data = tracts)
coef(m1)
No separate transformation step is needed.

Interpreting the coefficient
\[
\hat{\beta}_{\log(income)} = 502
\]
For a 1% increase in income:
\[
\frac{\beta}{100} = \frac{502}{100} \approx \$5
\]

A 1% increase in median income is associated with about $5 more rent, holding the other variables constant.

For a 10% increase in income:
\[
\beta \times \log(1.10) = 502 \times 0.0953 \approx \$48
\]

A 10% increase in income is associated with roughly $50 more rent.

Interpreting coefficients is not our main goal in prediction. But it is worth checking that they pass a sniff test.


Adding it to the model log
#| eval: false
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "M1: log(income)", rmse = cv_rmse(f1, tracts))


Result

The RMSE did not really improve.

A log transformation does not guarantee a better fit.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
14. Warning: Logs and Zeros
\[
\log(0) = -\infty
\]
If a variable contains real zeros, lm() will fail.
Example: counts of crimes or 311 calls per tract. A zero means “no crimes”. It is real information, not missing data.

Do not drop zero observations just to take a log.

Instead, use:
#| eval: false
log1p(x)
which computes:
\[
\log(1 + x)
\]
so that:
\[
\log(1 + 0) = 0
\]
The transcript records this as “log1px”. The correct R function is log1p().

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
15. Logging the Outcome Variable
If rent is skewed, we can log the outcome instead of, or as well as, the predictors.
#| eval: false
f2 <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age + dist_ch_mi
This is a log–log model for income.
You can go “log crazy”, but this is not recommended.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
16. Interpreting Log Models








Model
Form
Interpretation of β




Level–level
\(y \sim x\)
1-unit ↑ in x → β units change in y (the slope)


Level–log
\(y \sim \log(x)\)
1% ↑ in x → β / 100 units change in y


Log–level
\(\log(y) \sim x\)
1-unit ↑ in x → approx. 100 × β % change in y


Log–log
\(\log(y) \sim \log(x)\)
1% ↑ in x → approx. β % change in y



The log–log coefficient is an elasticity, a familiar idea from economics.
In the lecture, the level–level case was described as “a β percent increase in y”. The correct reading is β units of y.

You do not need to memorize these. Prediction is our main focus. But you should know where to look them up.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
17. Critical Warning: Log Dollars
When the outcome is logged, the RMSE suddenly looks amazing:
Before: RMSE ≈ 265
After:  RMSE ≈ 0.18
This is not a breakthrough.
The second number is in log dollars.

Your boss does not speak log dollars. They want to know how many dollars the model is off by.

So we must convert predictions back to dollars by taking the exponent:
\[
\hat{y} = e^{\widehat{\log(y)}}
\]
This is what the log_y = TRUE argument in cv_rmse() does:
#| eval: false
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(
    model = "M2: log(rent) + log(income)",
    rmse  = cv_rmse(f2, tracts, log_y = TRUE)
  )

Result

The RMSE improved by about $2.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
18. Trick 2: Squared (Polynomial) Terms

Non-linear relationships
If a scatter plot shows a curve, we can still use a linear model. We just “trick” it by adding a squared term.


Classic example: building age
New buildings      → higher rent (new and shiny; built in desirable areas)
Middle-aged        → lower rent (dated, not updated)
Very old buildings → higher rent again ("vintage")
So the relationship between age and rent is often U-shaped:
Rent
 │ ●                       ●
 │   ●                   ●
 │     ●             ●
 │        ●  ●  ●
 └──────────────────────────── Building age
   new     middle-aged     old


A data artifact to watch for
The Census records every building built before 1940 as “1939 or earlier”.
All of those tracts get the same value, which creates a pile-up at the oldest ages.

Discover artifacts like this through exploratory data analysis. Always plot your data (scatter plots!) after collecting it.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
section: 19. Adding a Squared Term with I()
text:
19. Adding a Squared Term with I()
#| eval: false
f3 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age +
  I(building_age^2) + dist_ch_mi

m3 <- lm(f3, data = tracts)
I() means “do the math”: compute building_age^2 as a new variable.

Without I(), R quietly ignores the squared term or gives a syntax error.

Keep both the linear term and the squared term in the model.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
20. Reading the Two Coefficients Together
The model now estimates:
\[
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x + \beta_2 x^2 + \dots
\]
The signs of \(\beta_1\) and \(\beta_2\) together describe the shape:



Linear term \(\beta_1\)
Squared term \(\beta_2\)
Shape




+
−
Rises, then levels off or falls (∩)


−
+
Falls, then rises (∪)



In our model:

\(\beta_1\) (building age) is negative → rent falls as buildings age
\(\beta_2\) (building age²) is positive → eventually rent rises again


This picks up the non-linear “vintage” pattern we expected.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
21. The Turning Point
Where does the effect switch from negative to positive?
\[
x^* = -\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}
\]
where:

\(\beta_1\) = coefficient on the linear term
\(\beta_2\) = coefficient on the squared term

#| eval: false
b1 <- coef(m3)["building_age"]
b2 <- coef(m3)["I(building_age^2)"]

turning_point <- -b1 / (2 * b2)
turning_point

Result
\[
x^* \approx 76.8 \text{ years}
\]

Around 77 years old, buildings become “vintage enough” that age starts to add to rent.



Check: is the turning point inside your data?
#| eval: false
max(tracts$building_age)
In our data, the maximum building age is about 85 years, so the turning point is within the observed range.
If the turning point were far outside your data (for example, 200 years), the parabola would only bend. It would not actually turn within the data.

Don’t tell a story about a turn you never observed.



Result
#| eval: false
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "M3: + building age²", rmse = cv_rmse(f3, tracts))

RMSE fell by about another $2, to roughly $261.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
22. Trick 3: Categorical Variables

Two reasons to use categories
1. The data already come in categories

Zoning class
Housing type
Inside a TOD area or not
Planning district

Categories may be binary (yes/no) or have several groups.
2. We create our own categories
When a continuous variable seems to behave like groups rather than a straight line.


Example: distance rings
Instead of assuming rent declines steadily with distance from City Hall, we might assume:



Ring
Distance from City Hall




Core
Under 2 miles


Inner
2 to under 5 miles


Outer
5 miles or more



The idea: being 0.2 miles or 2 miles from City Hall has roughly the same effect. Both are “core”.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
23. Creating Categories with case_when()
#| eval: false
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE           ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring)
  )

Conditions are checked in order
TRUE catches everyone else who did not meet the earlier conditions


Why factor()?
A factor tells R that the values are groups, not numbers.
This matters most when categories are labelled with numbers:
1, 2, 3
Without factor(), R treats them as ordinal or continuous numbers, as if 1 < 2 < 3.

Use factor() so categories are treated as labels, not quantities.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
24. Always Count Your Categories
#| eval: false
tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(ring)

This is where 99% of your cross-validation problems will come from.


Why?
Suppose only 3 tracts are in the core, and all three land in the same test fold:
Training data: no core tracts
        ↓
Model never estimates a coefficient for "Core"
        ↓
Test data: "We're core!"
        ↓
Model: "I've never heard of core" → error

Make sure every category has enough observations for both the regression and cross-validation.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
25. Evenly Spaced Bins with cut()
Instead of choosing thresholds from theory, cut() divides a variable into evenly spaced bins.
#| eval: false
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    renter_group = cut(
      pct_renters,
      breaks = 3,
      labels = c("Mostly Owners", "Mixed", "Mostly Renters")
    )
  )



Category
Number of tracts




Mostly Owners
88


Mixed
210


Mostly Renters
79


Total
377

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
section: 26. Dummy Coding and the Reference Category
text:
26. Dummy Coding and the Reference Category
Behind the scenes, R converts each category into binary (0/1) variables:



Tract
ring
Inner
Outer




A
Core
0
0


B
Inner
1
0


C
Outer
0
1



A tract that is neither Inner nor Outer must be Core.

Why k − 1?
Because of the math, a model cannot include all category dummies and an intercept.
With \(k\) categories, R estimates:
\[
k - 1
\]
dummy variables.
Here:
\[
k = 3 \quad (\text{Core, Inner, Outer}) \Rightarrow k - 1 = 2
\]
The left-out category is the reference category. Its effect is absorbed into the intercept.

Category coefficients are always interpreted relative to the reference category.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
27. Interpreting Category Coefficients
#| eval: false
f4 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age +
  I(building_age^2) + ring

m4 <- lm(f4, data = tracts)
coef(m4)








Ring
Coefficient
Interpretation




Core
Reference
(absorbed in intercept)


Inner
−122
Inner-ring tracts rent for $122 less than core tracts, all else equal


Outer
−164
Outer-ring tracts rent for $164 less than core tracts, all else equal




Changing the reference category
By default, R chooses the reference alphabetically (“Core” comes first).
#| eval: false
tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(ring = relevel(ring, ref = "Outer"))
Now the interpretation becomes:

Compared with the outer ring, core tracts rent for about $160 more.


Changing the reference category changes the interpretation, not the predictions.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
28. Trade-off: Categories Throw Away Information
Replacing continuous distance with three rings means:
2.1 miles → Inner
4.9 miles → Inner
Both are treated identically, even though they are almost 3 miles apart.
You can include both the continuous variable and the categories, but check that this does not destabilize the model.

Result
#| eval: false
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "M4: rings instead of distance", rmse = cv_rmse(f4, tracts))

The RMSE got worse.

It was not a great example, but it does not hurt to try. Consider categories when:

The data look jumpy or grouped
You have a strong theoretical reason

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
29. Trick 4: Interaction Terms

Categories vs. interactions







Technique
What changes by group?




Categorical variable
The intercept (the level shifts up or down)


Interaction term
The slope (the relationship itself differs)





Hypothesis
The relationship between income and rent may differ by ring:

Steeper in Center City
Flatter further out, where income matters less



Code
Multiply the terms inside the formula:
#| eval: false
f5 <- rent ~ log(income) * ring + pct_renters +
  building_age + I(building_age^2)

m5 <- lm(f5, data = tracts)
coef(m5)
log(income) * ring includes:

log(income) main effect
ring main effects
log(income):ring interaction terms

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
30. Interpreting Interaction Coefficients








Term
Coefficient
Meaning




log(income)
653
Slope in the Core (reference)


log(income):ringInner
−219
Inner-ring slope is 219 less → ≈ 434


log(income):ringOuter
−244
Outer-ring slope is 244 less → ≈ 409



So the income–rent relationship is indeed strongest in the core.

Result
#| eval: false
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "M5: log(income) × ring", rmse = cv_rmse(f5, tracts))

RMSE ≈ $264: better than M4, but worse than the best model so far.


Use interactions when you have a reason, not “willy-nilly”. Models quickly become untenable.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
31. Trick 5: Fixed Effects

The idea
Suppose you have included everything you can measure:

Distance to the core
Income
Share of people with a bachelor’s degree
Bike share stations
…

There may still be unmeasurable factors that explain why rent is higher in some places:

Sense of place
Perception
Reputation

A fixed effect is a catch-all:

A dummy variable for an area that absorbs the remaining variation explained simply by being located there.



Choosing the area
Our outcome is already measured at the tract level, so the fixed effect must be a larger area.
We use Philadelphia’s:

18 planning districts

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
32. Assigning Tracts to Planning Districts
#| eval: false
districts <- st_read("planning_districts.geojson") %>%
  st_transform(2272)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  st_join(
    districts %>% select(district = DIST_NAME),
    largest = TRUE
  ) %>%
  mutate(district = factor(district))
The file name and the DIST_NAME field are illustrative. Use the names in the course code.

Spatial join with largest = TRUE
What if a tract is split by two districts?
┌───────────────┐
│ District 1    │ District 2
│   ███████████ │ ████
│   ███ tract ██│ ████
└───────────────┘
largest = TRUE assigns the whole tract to the district containing the largest share of its area.

Unlike st_intersection(), the tract is not cut. It receives one district value.



Why factor() again?
District numbers are labels, not rankings. District 1 is not “less than” District 2.

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
33. Small Categories Break Cross-Validation
#| eval: false
tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(district, sort = TRUE)
In the lecture, one district (Lower South) contained very few tracts.
This caused two problems:

When those tracts were in the test fold, the training model had never learned their coefficient → error
Estimating a coefficient from one observation is highly unstable


Fix

Make sure every category has at least about 10 observations.

Options:

Combine small categories into an “Other” group (works, but not ideal)
Merge a small district with a neighbouring district (better)

#| eval: false
small <- tracts %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  count(district) %>%
  filter(n < 10) %>%
  pull(district)

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    district = as.character(district),
    district = if_else(district %in% small, "Other", district),
    district = factor(district)
  )

title: Week 7: Feature Engineering for Linear Regression
text:
34. Estimating the Fixed Effects Model
#| eval: false
f6 <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renters + building_age +
  I(building_age^2) + dist_ch_mi + district

m6 <- lm(f6, data = tracts)
Here the fixed effects are added to the best model so far. Check the course code for the exact formula.

What do we get?
Each district gets its own intercept.
Mapping these intercepts shows the “value” of being in each district, which is useful information in itself.


Did the fixed effects absorb spatial clustering?
Comparing maps of residuals before and after adding district fixed effects shows only minor differences.


Result
#| eval: false
model_log <- model_log %>%
  add_row(model = "M6: + district fixed effects",
          rmse  = cv_rmse(f6, tracts, log_y = TRUE))

RMSE ≈ $256: the best model.


Adding fixed effects is a reliable way to lower RMSE in geographic price prediction.

The lecturer also mentioned her research modelling neighbourhood fixed effects for Chicago. Ask about it in class.

text:
38. Key Concepts to Remember

Linear regression fits a straight line, but feature engineering lets it capture more complex relationships.
Linear regression is interpretable. More complex methods are not automatically better.
Feature engineering means operationalizing ideas (such as “closeness to Center City”) as measurable variables.
Create points from latitude/longitude in EPSG:4326, then transform to the project CRS.
lm() quietly drops rows with missing values, so filter NAs before comparing models.
Compare models using the same records and the same folds.
A model log is a record of models and RMSEs, not a logarithm.
Log transformations help with skewed data and when percentage changes matter.
log(0) is −∞. Use log1p() for variables with real zeros.
With a logged outcome, back-transform predictions with exp() before computing RMSE. Otherwise the error is in log dollars.
Log–log coefficients are elasticities.
Squared terms, written with I(x^2), capture curved relationships.
Read the linear and squared coefficients together to understand the shape.
The turning point is −β₁ / (2β₂). Check that it falls inside the data range.
Always do exploratory analysis. The Census groups all pre-1940 buildings as “1939 or earlier”.
Use factor() so categories are treated as groups, not numbers.
Categorical variables are dummy coded into k − 1 variables. The omitted group is the reference category.
Category coefficients are interpreted relative to the reference. Changing the reference changes interpretation, not predictions.
Turning a continuous variable into categories throws away information.
Categorical variables shift the intercept. Interaction terms let the slope vary by group.
Use interactions only when you have a reason.
Fixed effects absorb unmeasured characteristics of place, such as reputation and sense of place.
st_join(..., largest = TRUE) assigns each polygon to the area containing most of it.
Always count observations per category. Small categories break cross-validation. Aim for at least ~10.
Fixed effects gave the best model (≈ $256 RMSE).

2. Recap: Reading a Logged Predictor
From the Week 7 lecture (Oct 9), we predicted tract rent using the log of median income:

Reading the coefficient (\(\hat{\beta}\))
A 1% increase in income goes with about:
\[

more rent.

Logging income lets the model bend. It flattens out at high incomes, so it does not over-predict rent in the richest tracts.

11. From “By Eye” to a Number
In the Week 5 lab and the gap assignment, we compared residual maps before and after adding features, by eye.
Today we put a number on the question:

Do the errors cluster?


Tobler’s First Law of Geography

“Near things are more related than distant things.”

Applied to model errors:

If near houses have related errors, the model is missing something about place.

When errors are random in space, the model has captured location well. When red errors sit together and blue errors sit together, something about those places is not in the model.

Step by step (all functions from spdep):








Step
Function
What it does




1
st_coordinates()
Get the x, y coordinates of each house


2
knearneigh(coords, k = 5)
Find each house’s 5 nearest houses


3
knn2nb()
Turn that into a neighbor list


4
nb2listw(..., style = "W")
Turn neighbors into weights. "W" = row-standardized: each neighbor gets weight 1/5


5

For each house, compute the weighted average of its neighbors’ residuals




Each house gets the average residual of its 5 nearest neighbors. This is the “spatial lag”.

text:
14. Moran’s I: The “Scary” Formula
\[
I = \frac{n}{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}} \cdot
\frac{\sum_i \sum_j w_{ij}(x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})}
     {\sum_i (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
\]
where:

\(n\) = number of observations
\(x_i\) = the value (here, the residual) at location \(i\)
\(\bar{x}\) = the mean value
\(w_{ij}\) = the weight between \(i\) and \(j\) (non-zero if they are neighbors)


What it is really asking

When I’m above average, are my neighbors above average too?

Breaking down the parts:







Part
Meaning




\((x_i - \bar{x})(x_j - \bar{x})\)
Positive if neighbors are on the same side of the mean, negative if they differ


\(\sum \sum w_{ij}(\dots)\)
Add this up over all neighbor pairs


\(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2\)
Divide by the total variation, to scale it


\(n / \sum \sum w_{ij}\)
Adjust for the number of observations and links

17. Is That Big? Shuffle and See
#| eval: false
mc <- moran.mc(sales$resid, w_knn, nsim = 499)

mc$statistic
mc$p.value
statistic
0.2605251

[1] 0.002

How the permutation test works
Compute the real Moran's I
        ↓
Shuffle the residuals randomly across houses (499 times)
        ↓
Compute Moran's I for every shuffle
        ↓
Does the real I beat almost all the shuffles?
        ↓
If yes → the clustering isn't luck
With 499 shuffles, the smallest possible p-value is:
\[
\frac{1}{499 + 1} = 0.002
\]
So \(p = 0.002\) means the real I was larger than every shuffle.
Here, I ≈ 0.26: moderate clustering of errors that is clearly not random.

text:
20. “My Spatial Stats Class Says Use a Spatial Lag Model”
A spatial lag model puts neighbors’ outcomes on the right-hand side:
\[
y = \rho W y + X\beta + \varepsilon
\]
where \(Wy\) is the average price of neighboring houses and \(\rho\) measures how strongly it matters.
That is the right tool for inference about spillovers (for example, “does a house’s price depend on its neighbors’ prices?”).
For prediction, it fails in three ways:

It needs neighbors’ prices. To price a house, you would need the prices of nearby houses that have not sold yet.
It leaks. In cross-validation, a test house’s neighbors in the training set carry its answer.
It explains nothing. “It’s near expensive houses” is not a reason a policymaker can act on.


Our rule

Spatial features of X, never Y.




Allowed
Not allowed




Crime near the house
Prices near the house


Distance to transit, parks, City Hall
Neighbors’ sale prices

title: Week 8: Where Is the Model Wrong? Spatial Autocorrelation and Spatial Modelling
text:
27. Key Concepts to Remember

With a logged predictor and Y in dollars, β / 100 is the change in Y for a 1% change in X.
Small categories break cross-validation. Merge small groups before CV. The same problem returns with ~150 neighborhoods.
House price prediction uses the same tools as before, but the unit is a point (sale) rather than a polygon (tract).
A buffer is a polygon you draw yourself.
Not every sale is a market sale. $1 transfers, sheriff sales and LLC shuffles are recorded too.
Deciding what counts as a market sale is a modeling decision. Write it down.
A buffer count can be zero for many houses. A kNN distance is never zero. Let CV RMSE decide between them.
Residual = actual − predicted. Positive (red) = under-predicted. Negative (blue) = over-predicted.
Use transparency and squished colour limits so a few huge misses do not wash out a residual map.
Tobler: near things are more related than distant things.
If nearby houses have related errors, the model is missing something about place.
The spatial lag is the average value among a location’s neighbors.
The slope of the Moran scatterplot (my residual vs. neighbors’ average) is Moran’s I with row-standardized weights.
Moran’s I asks: when I’m above average, are my neighbors above average too?
Moran’s I near +1 = clustering. Near 0 = no pattern. Below 0 = neighbors differ (rare for errors; check weights).
moran.mc() tests significance by shuffling values across locations.
With ~20,000 houses, nearly everything is significant. Watch the size of I fall, not the p-value.
Clustered errors point to a missing spatial feature, a neighborhood fixed effect, or an interaction.
Spatial lag models are for inference about spillovers, not prediction. They need unsold neighbors’ prices, they leak in CV, and they explain nothing.
Spatial features of X, never Y.

If CV RMSE and test RMSE are far apart, something leaked.

We also look at price against building age. We want to see whether a straight-line relationship seems reasonable or whether we should test age squared as well. We do not remove a house just because it is old. Again, the log price axis is only for the plot.


Code

  geom_point(alpha = .12, size = .6, color = "#287D8E") +
  scale_y_log10(labels = money) + labs(x = "Building age (years)", y = "Sale price (log display)")





Prices vary widely within building ages; age alone is not a cleaning rule.




Finally, we map the sales to see where higher and lower prices cluster. Each point is a sale, and the color shows its price. If prices vary across the city, we have a reason to test location features alongside house characteristics. The map alone cannot explain why those differences exist. We use a log color scale so a few expensive sales do not dominate the colors.


Code

  scale_color_viridis_c(trans = "log10", labels = money, name = "Sale price") +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL)





Cleaned training sales. Color uses a logarithmic price scale; no expensive records are hidden.




Answer: What in your exploration shaped your modeling choices?
Houses with similar sizes sell for very different prices, so we did not expect house characteristics alone to explain everything. We started with a structure-only model, then tested squared size and age terms and an alternative using log size. The map also gave us a reason to test location features. We used cross-validation to check whether those additions helped.
We kept the unusually low and high prices because we did not have enough evidence to call them errors. That choice has consequences: expensive sales can drive dollar RMSE, while a relatively small dollar error can be a large percentage of a cheap house’s price. We return to both issues in Part 4.

Cross-validation and spatial weights
This loop follows Week 7. We fill missing predictors using the fitting rows before calling lm(). We keep the raw predictions, including negative values, when we calculate error. We do not replace them with zero. Negative predictions show where this linear model gives an impossible house value.


Code
cv_predictions <- function(formula, data, fold_id) {
  predictions <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))

  for (k in 1:10) {
    validation <- fold_id == k
    fitting <- fill_missing(data[!validation, ], data[!validation, ])
    validating <- fill_missing(data[validation, ], data[!validation, ])

    fit <- lm(formula, data = fitting)
    predictions[validation] <- predict(fit, newdata = validating)
  }

  predictions
}

morans_i <- function(values, weights) {
  moran(values, weights, n = length(values), S0 = Szero(weights))$I
}

The LISA maps identify places for further investigation. We would need to check the data in those places before choosing a new neighborhood feature. text:
Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)

Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?

We started with house characteristics, then added location because similar houses can sell for different prices across Chicago. We compared squared terms, log size, distance, rings, interactions and tract fixed effects. Adding tract-specific size slopes and an age-by-ring interaction gave the lowest CV RMSE among the tested formulas. We chose among them using the same grouped CV folds. These fitted relationships describe associations; they do not tell us what changing a house or neighborhood would cause.
Our central-air coefficient is $17,524. As beta-hat, it is the estimated price difference between the supplied central-air categories, holding the other predictors fixed. For y-hat, switching that indicator from 0 to 1 changes the predicted price by that amount. We cannot interpret it as the return from installing air conditioning because condition and renovations may also differ between houses.
We would not give this model to the Assessor for operational use yet. It improves on the baseline, but the residual maps and LISA results show where further checks are needed. Dollar RMSE can hide large proportional errors for inexpensive houses. Income-group comparisons help us describe that concern, but tract income is not an owner’s income and cannot establish individual fairness.
We removed bundled transactions rather than guessing how to divide their prices. We kept both price tails because we could not justify excluding them. Grouping rounded coordinates helps with repeated sales, but verified parcel IDs would be better. Our CV score also influenced model selection, so it is not an independent final test. Before using this model for assessments, we would evaluate a later year and held-out geographic areas, verify condition and transaction details, and investigate impossible predictions. We would follow Week 8’s approach of checking residual clusters and measuring a plausible missing feature before adding it. We should not assume a more complicated model will fix every error.

4. Local Moran’s I: One House at a Time
\[
I_i = \frac{z_i}{m_2} \sum_j w_{ij} z_j
\qquad
m_2 = \frac{\sum_i z_i^2}{n} = \frac{22{,}920}{5} = 4{,}584
\]
where:

\(z_i\) = my deviation from the mean
\(\sum_j w_{ij} z_j\) = my neighbors’ average deviation (with row-standardized weights)
\(m_2\) = the average squared deviation, used to scale the result

In words:

Local Moran’s I = me × my neighbors’ average, scaled.


Worked values

For example, for house A:
\[
I_A = \frac{84 \times 64}{4{,}584} = \frac{5{,}376}{4{,}584} \approx 1.17
\]


Link to the global value
The average of the five local values is:
\[
\frac{1.17 + 0.61 + 0.00 + 0.59 + 1.24}{5} \approx 0.72
\]
This is the global Moran’s I with these weights.

Global Moran’s I is the average of the local Moran’s I values.



Why 0.72 and not 0.60 like last week?

Last week we used plain 0/1 (binary) neighbor weights → I ≈ 0.60
spdep with style = "W" averages the neighbors (row-standardized) → I ≈ 0.72

Same story, different weighting.

text:
6. Last Week’s Model, Out-of-Fold Residuals
We rebuild last week’s Philadelphia model: same sales, same cleaning rules, same violent-crime feature.
#| eval: false
sales <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom, parcel_number, sale_price, sale_date, total_livable_area,
          number_of_bedrooms, number_of_bathrooms, year_built, interior_condition
   FROM opa_properties_public
   WHERE category_code = '1'
     AND sale_date >= '2023-01-01' AND sale_date < '2025-01-01'"
) %>%
  st_transform(2272) %>%
  filter(sale_price >= 10000, total_livable_area > 0, !st_is_empty(.)) %>%
  mutate(year_built = na_if(as.numeric(year_built), 0),
         age = 2024 - year_built) %>%
  filter(!is.na(age), !is.na(number_of_bathrooms))

violent <- carto_get(
  "SELECT the_geom FROM incidents_part1_part2
   WHERE dispatch_date >= '2023-01-01' AND dispatch_date < '2025-01-01'
     AND text_general_code IN ('Aggravated Assault Firearm',
                               'Aggravated Assault No Firearm',
                               'Robbery Firearm', 'Robbery No Firearm')"
) %>%
  filter(!st_is_empty(.)) %>%
  st_transform(2272)

sales$violent_knn5 <- sapply(
  st_nn(sales, violent, k = 5, returnDist = TRUE, progress = FALSE)$dist,
  mean
)

f1 <- sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age + violent_knn5

sales$resid_1 <- sales$sale_price - cv_pred(f1, sales)
cv_pred() and cv_rmse() are course helper functions. cv_pred() returns each house’s cross-validated prediction.

What’s new: out-of-fold residuals
Last week, residuals came from a model fitted on all houses. Now:

Each house’s error comes from the fold where it was held out.

This gives an honest picture of how the model performs on houses it has not seen, which is how it will be used.

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
7. Local Moran’s I in R
#| eval: false
library(spdep)

w_knn <- nb2listw(
  knn2nb(knearneigh(st_coordinates(sales), k = 5)),
  style = "W"
)

lisa_quads <- function(resid, w, alpha = 0.01) {
  lm_perm <- localmoran_perm(resid, w, nsim = 499)
  z   <- resid - mean(resid)
  lag <- lag.listw(w, z)
  p   <- lm_perm[, "Pr(z != E(Ii)) Sim"]
  case_when(
    p >= alpha      ~ "Not significant",
    z > 0 & lag > 0 ~ "High-High",
    z < 0 & lag < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
    z > 0 & lag < 0 ~ "High-Low",
    TRUE            ~ "Low-High"
  )
}

sales$quad_1 <- lisa_quads(sales$resid_1, w_knn)
table(sales$quad_1)
The weights are the same as last week: each house’s 5 nearest sales, row-standardized.

What lisa_quads() does








Step
Code
Meaning




1
localmoran_perm(resid, w, nsim = 499)
Local Moran’s I for every house, with a permutation (shuffle) test


2
z <- resid - mean(resid)
Am I above or below the average error?


3
lag <- lag.listw(w, z)
Are my neighbors above or below average?


4
p <- ...Sim
The simulated p-value for each house


5
case_when(...)
Assign each house to a quadrant, or “Not significant” if p ≥ 0.01



The significance threshold is α = 0.01, stricter than the usual 0.05, because we are running thousands of tests.

10. Who’s in the Blue?
Low–Low means over-predicted.

As an assessment, an over-predicted house is an over-taxed house.

So we ask: are the over-predicted pockets in poorer or richer neighborhoods?
#| eval: false
tract_inc <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract", variables = "B19013_001",   # median household income
  state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia", year = 2023,
  geometry = TRUE, progress = FALSE
) %>%

  select(med_inc = estimate)

  st_join(tract_inc, join = st_nearest_feature) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  filter(!is.na(med_inc)) %>%
  mutate(inc_quintile = ntile(med_inc, 5)) %>%
  group_by(inc_quintile) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    pct_low_low   = mean(quad_1 == "Low-Low") * 100,
    pct_high_high = mean(quad_1 == "High-High") * 100

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
11. Global vs. Local Moran’s I









Global Moran’s I
Local Moran’s I (LISA)




Output
One number
One number per house


Question
Do errors cluster?
Where do they cluster?


Use
Model log: did it fall?
To-do list: what’s missing there?


Danger
p-value always tiny with a big n
Thousands of tests, so some clusters appear by chance



The LISA danger is a multiple-testing problem. At α = 0.05, about 1 in 20 tests would be “significant” even with no real pattern. That is one reason the function uses the stricter α = 0.01.

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
12. Operationalizing “Near” (Word of the Week)
To operationalize a concept is to turn it into something we can measure.
“Near violent crime” can be measured in three ways:









Method
How
Good when
Watch out




Buffer count
Incidents within 660 ft
Exposure: “how much is around me?”
Zeros everywhere. The radius is a choice


Nearest distance
Feet to the single closest
One thing matters: a station, a park
One odd point decides everything


kNN mean distance
Mean feet to the 5 closest
Smooth intensity. Never zero
k is a choice. Far-away points count



All three are features of X: none of them uses a price. That follows last week’s rule: spatial features of X, never Y.
You have already built the buffer count and kNN distance. Nearest distance is new.

Logging a distance
Distances often matter in relative terms (rates of change):
100 ft → 500 ft     a big difference (next door vs. down the block)
5,000 ft → 5,400 ft no real difference (both are far away)
Taking the log of a distance captures this: the same raw change matters more when you are close.

13. Building All Three Features
#| eval: false
sales <- sales %>%
  mutate(
    violent_660ft = lengths(st_intersects(st_buffer(., 660), violent)),
    violent_near  = as.numeric(st_distance(
      ., violent[st_nearest_feature(., violent), ],
      by_element = TRUE
    )),
    log_violent_knn5 = log(violent_knn5)
  )

How the new feature works







Function
What it does




st_nearest_feature(., violent)
For each house, the index of the closest crime


violent[...]
Pulls out that closest crime for each house


st_distance(..., by_element = TRUE)
Distance from each house to its own nearest crime, one pair at a time (not a full matrix)


as.numeric()
Drops the units, leaving feet





Let cross-validation choose
#| eval: false
structure_f <- "sale_price ~ total_livable_area + number_of_bathrooms + age"

tibble(feature = c("violent_660ft", "violent_near",
                   "violent_knn5", "log_violent_knn5")) %>%
  mutate(cv_rmse = map_dbl(
    feature,
    ~ cv_rmse(as.formula(paste(structure_f, "+", .x)), sales)
  )) %>%
  arrange(cv_rmse)
This loops over the four candidates. Each time it adds one crime feature to the same structural model and records the CV RMSE.
  feature          cv_rmse
1 violent_knn5     432287
2 violent_near     432295
3 log_violent_knn5 432300
4 violent_660ft    432314


Interpretation

kNN mean distance wins, but the four are within about $27 of each other.
The way you operationalize “near” matters much less here than whether you include crime at all.
The RMSE is large (over $430,000), most likely because of very expensive sales in the data. RMSE squares the errors, so a few big misses dominate it.

text:
14. Choosing k and the Radius

Decide your short list before you look.

Pick 2–3 values with a reason, then let CV RMSE choose among them:

A city block is about 500 ft
1/8 mile (660 ft) is a short walk

Why decide first? If you try dozens of values and keep the best, you are tuning to noise. The CV RMSE then looks better than the model really is.

text:
15. A Feature Aimed at a Cluster
Suppose the blue (Low–Low) pockets look like blocks with a lot of vacancy. We can measure that with the ACS:
#| eval: false
tract_vac <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(total = "B25002_001", vacant = "B25002_003"),
  state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia", year = 2023,
  geometry = TRUE, output = "wide", progress = FALSE
) %>%
  st_transform(2272) %>%
  transmute(pct_vacant = if_else(totalE > 0, vacantE / totalE * 100, NA_real_))

sales <- sales %>%
  st_join(tract_vac, join = st_nearest_feature) %>%
  mutate(pct_vacant = replace_na(pct_vacant, median(pct_vacant, na.rm = TRUE)))

f2 <- update(f1, . ~ . + pct_vacant)

sales$resid_2 <- sales$sale_price - cv_pred(f2, sales)
sales$quad_2  <- lisa_quads(sales$resid_2, w_knn)







Step
Meaning




B25002_001, B25002_003
Total housing units and vacant units (ACS table B25002)


if_else(totalE > 0, ...)
Avoid dividing by zero in tracts with no housing


replace_na(..., median(...))
Fill missing vacancy with the median, so every row is kept


update(f1, . ~ . + pct_vacant)
Same formula as f1, plus vacancy



replace_na() keeps every row (Rule 1: all models must use the same records).

Filling in missing values is a choice. Log it.

section: 17. How to Use These Statistics: The Workflow
text:
17. How to Use These Statistics: The Workflow
1. Fit the model → get OUT-OF-FOLD residuals
        ↓
2. Global Moran's I → a quick overall check: do the errors cluster?
        ↓
3. LISA map → spots that could use patching up
        ↓
4. Ask what's there → measure it (buffer, nearest, or kNN)
        ↓
5. Refit → log CV RMSE and Moran's I. Did that cluster shrink?
        ↓
6. Repeat, until the clusters you can explain are gone
   (or you've spent enough time on it)

text:
18. Should We Build This?
You have spent two weeks building a model that predicts what a home is worth from what it is and where it is.
Now imagine a company sells that model to landlords, with rent as the outcome.
Three questions to keep in mind:

What goes into the model, and who supplied it?
Who acts on the prediction, and can they say no?
Who pays when it’s wrong? Who pays when it’s right?

Film shown in class: How RealPage influences rent prices (CNBC, 2024, about 10 minutes).

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
19. What the RealPage Software Does
INPUTS
  • Public listings and market data
  • The landlord's own leases
  • Competing landlords' NONPUBLIC leases, rents, occupancy
        ↓
MODEL
  Predict rent
        ↓
OUTPUT
  A recommended rent for every unit, every day
        ↓
DECISION
  Leasing manager accepts or overrides (auto-accept available)

The modeling is our house price assignment with rent instead of price.

The fight is not about the regression. It is about:

The third input: data competitors would never share with each other directly
The last arrow: how hard it is to say no to the recommendation

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
20. The Debate









Critics: DOJ, tenants, Philadelphia
Defenders: RealPage, landlords




Data
Pooling rivals’ private rents lets competitors align prices without ever talking
About two-thirds of inputs are public. Private data is aggregated and anonymized


Prices
Recommendations push rents up, and hold them up when demand falls
Rents rose because of the supply shortage, inflation and interest rates. The software cuts rents when demand drops


Humans
Alleged auto-accept and “pricing advisors” who pressed managers to comply. Ex-employees told ProPublica ~90% of recommendations were adopted
Managers set a different price more than half the time


Reach
A law professor estimates 30–60% of multifamily units in 40+ markets
The company says 7% of U.S. rentals


Efficiency
—
Overpriced units sit empty. Better pricing fills them



Sources cited in the slides: DOJ complaint as reported by Axios and Groundwork Collaborative (2024); ProPublica (2022).

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
21. Where It Stands

Federal
The U.S. Department of Justice sued RealPage in August 2024.
The November 2025 settlement (filed November 24, 2025; described in the lecture as now approved by the court) requires:

No competitors’ nonpublic data when setting prices
Training on nonpublic data only if it is at least 12 months old
No geographic effects finer than the state
Removal of features that limited price cuts or aligned competitors’ prices, plus a court-appointed monitor

It also:

Includes no admission of wrongdoing
Lets RealPage keep selling the product



Philadelphia

City Council unanimously banned rent-coordination software in October 2024, in effect from February 2025.
The first tenant lawsuits under the ordinance were filed in July 2026, against Greystar, Bozzuto, Willow Bridge, RealPage and Yardi.
The allegations are unproven.

title: Week 9: Local Spatial Autocorrelation (LISA), Operationalizing “Near”, and the Case of RealPage
text:
29. Key Concepts to Remember

Global Moran’s I answers whether errors cluster. Local Moran’s I (LISA) answers where.
Local Moran’s I is me × my neighbors’ average, scaled. The average of the local values is the global I.
With row-standardized weights the five-house example gives I ≈ 0.72. With binary 0/1 weights it gives 0.60. Same story, different weighting.
High–High = pocket the model under-predicts (missing amenity). Low–Low = pocket it over-predicts (missing disamenity).
High–Low and Low–High are outliers. They point to the house, not the place.
Clusters → build a spatial feature. Outliers → check the data.
Use out-of-fold residuals: each house’s error comes from the fold where it was held out.
LISA runs thousands of tests, so chance clusters appear. Use a strict threshold (here α = 0.01).
Plot non-significant houses first so clusters sit on top.
For each cluster, ask: where is it, what’s there, can I measure it?
Over-predicted = over-taxed. In Philadelphia, Low–Low clusters were about 10× more common in the poorest income quintile than the richest: a regressive pattern.
Operationalize “near” in three ways: buffer count, nearest distance, kNN mean distance. All are features of X.
Logging a distance captures that close changes matter more than far ones.
Decide your short list of k and radius values before you look, then let CV RMSE choose.
Filling missing values with replace_na() keeps every row, but it is a choice: log it.
If a new feature doesn’t shrink the cluster you aimed at, your guess was wrong. That’s information too.
Workflow: fit → out-of-fold residuals → global I → LISA map → measure what’s there → refit → log CV RMSE and Moran’s I → repeat.
RealPage’s model is technically the same as ours. The controversy is about pooled nonpublic competitor data and how hard it is to override the recommendation.
The DOJ settlement bans nonpublic competitor data when setting prices, limits training to data 12+ months old, and bans geography finer than the state.
Philadelphia banned rent-coordination software in 2024. The first tenant suits under it came in July 2026; the allegations are unproven.
Three questions for any predictive model: what’s in the data, who can say no, and who pays?
An accurate prediction can still be the problem.
